biography.education: B.S., Florida A&M University; J.D., Georgia State University College of Law
biography.background: Attorney. Fifth-generation Georgian. Daughter of R&B musician Major Lance. First Atlanta mayor to serve in all three branches of city government (judge, council member, mayor). Led Atlanta through COVID-19 pandemic, George Floyd unrest, 2020 election, and a major city cyberattack. If elected, would be the first Black woman governor in U.S. history.

keyActions.detail: Described the shooting as 'murder.' Issued Executive Order mandating de-escalation training, duty-to-intervene policy for officers, and use-of-force policy revision. Retained Police Executive Research Forum (PERF) for 'top to bottom review' of APD policy and training. Fired the officer. Said officers should be 'guardians, not warriors.'
Signed ordinance 18-O-1045 within weeks of taking office, eliminating cash bonds for city ordinance violations. Stated: 'People should not be held in jail because they cannot pay bond.'
Signed legislation authorizing closure of ACDC. Proposed reimagining it as a 'Center for Equity' providing residents with tools for success rather than incarceration.

Signed two executive orders: first prohibiting ACDC from accepting new ICE detainees; then permanently ending all ICE detainee agreements. Stated holding ICE detainees was 'untenable' and 'complicit in inhumane immigration policies.' Noted state law prevented declaring Atlanta a full sanctuary city.

Unveiled Atlanta's clean energy plan targeting 100% clean energy for municipal operations by 2025 and community-wide by 2035. Testified before the U.S. Senate Democrats' Special Committee on Climate Crisis (July 2019) — only Southern mayor on the panel. Cited 26,000 ER asthma visits/year in Atlanta. Joined Paris Agreement commitments despite federal withdrawal.

Plan aimed to create or preserve 20,000 affordable homes by 2026, raise $1 billion public-private. Proposed inclusionary zoning, ADU legalization, elimination of minimum parking requirements, second units on single-family lots, redevelopment of vacant public land for affordable housing.
keyActions.direction: supply expansion / government subsidies / loosen zoning

keyActions.detail: Partnered with MARTA Board to unanimously approve More MARTA Atlanta program — described as the region's largest transit investment in more than four decades.

keyActions.action: One Atlanta Economic Mobility, Recovery and Resiliency Plan (2020)
keyActions.detail: Plan focused on five objectives: Creation of Good Jobs, Access to Good Jobs, Small Businesses, Neighborhood Investment, and Affordable Housing. Targeted Black and brown communities with high poverty and unemployment.

Created city's first LGBTQ advisory board (2018). Released first LGBTQ Affairs report (February 2020). Appointed city's first director of LGBTQ Affairs (December 2020). City achieved perfect score on HRC Municipal Equality Index every year under Bottoms. First-ever city allocation of funds to combat HIV.

keyActions.action: Signed bipartisan mayor gun safety letter (2019); joined Moms Demand Action/Everytown advocacy
keyActions.detail: Signed U.S. Conference of Mayors letter (214 bipartisan mayors) after El Paso/Dayton mass shootings, urging universal background checks and limits on secondary sales. Called on Georgia state leaders to address 'lax gun laws.' Personal loss: nephew Darius killed in gun violence. Participated in Everytown/Moms Demand Action Veepstakes 2020. Simultaneously increased APD staffing and budget during crime surge.

keyActions.action: Four balanced budgets without tax increases (2018–2022)
keyActions.detail: Delivered four consecutive balanced budgets during COVID without property tax increases, layoffs, or furloughs. Left city reserves near historic high of $181M. Gave historic pay raises to police and firefighters.

keyActions.action: Crime surge and decision not to seek reelection (2020–2021)
keyActions.detail: Homicides, rapes, and auto thefts rose during her tenure. APD had 400 unfilled positions. Critics blamed COVID-era morale crisis and Rayshard Brooks fallout for officer departures. Bottoms offered retention bonuses and 13% pay increase for 911 operators. Announced in May 2021 she would not seek reelection — sources attributed partly to political cost of crime wave and reform-vs-safety tensions.
keyActions.direction: NOTE: Record is mixed — simultaneously reformed and funded APD; faced real public safety degradation

positionConflicts.topic: police accountability vs. public safety record
positionConflicts.conflict: Bottoms implemented significant APD reforms (use-of-force, de-escalation, civilian oversight), closed the city jail, and eliminated cash bail — positioning herself as a reformer. At the same time, crime rose significantly during her tenure (homicides, rapes, auto thefts), APD had 400 vacancies, and she simultaneously requested $13M more in police funding and gave officers historic pay raises. She chose not to seek reelection in part due to the political cost of the crime surge. In the 2026 race, she is 'reframing her record' to emphasize stability and executive competence over the reform framing.

positionConflicts.topic: immigration position as governor vs. state law constraints
positionConflicts.conflict: As mayor, Bottoms explicitly said state law prevented Atlanta from becoming a 'sanctuary city' even while she banned ICE detainees from the city jail. As a gubernatorial candidate, she has not specified what immigration enforcement posture she would take as governor — but her mayoral executive orders and Trump-opposition framing signal continued opposition to aggressive federal immigration enforcement.

evidenceSummary.notes: Bottoms has one of the most documented mayoral records of any 2026 state-level challenger nationally. Four years of executive decisions on policing, housing, climate, immigration, and criminal justice provide strong evidence across most axes. The 2026 campaign adds explicit commitments on Medicaid, abortion, housing, and education. Main gaps are on state-level specifics where her mayoral record does not directly translate (school choice policy, state energy portfolio, state sentencing). The one significant nuance: her policing record is mixed — she was simultaneously a reformer and a 'fund the police' mayor, and the crime surge contributed to her not seeking reelection. The scorer should flag this and not score her at either extreme of the police_accountability axis without noting the complexity.
